newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - Would-be Hong Kong leader Simon Li is hometown boy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Would-be Hong Kong leader Simon Li is hometown boy.

text.p: Simon Li, at 74 the oldest of four leading contenders to become Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader, is the only one born and bred in the territory.

"I'm a Hong Konger. I have a sense of responsibility and feelings towards Hong Kong," the retired appeal court judge noted with evident pride as he joined the contest to succeed Britain's Governor Chris Patten when Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30, 1997.
Li's three main rivals, former Chief Justice Ti Liang Yang, shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa and businessman Peter Woo, all have their roots in pre-communist Shanghai.

Unlike many of his fellow Hong Kongers who worry about possible erosion of human rights and lifestyle standards when the Chinese take over, Li has no qualms about how Hong Kong will fare when the red, five-starred Chinese flag replaces the Union Jack.
Asked in an interview with the South China Morning Post whether the post-1997 ideal of a prosperous, stable and harmonious society would be difficult to achieve, Li said: "It will be easy."
He said the relationship between Hong Kong and mainland China would be "more than one of lips and teeth".
"I can't imagine (they) will cut the nose to have a better-looking face. They won't rock the boat."

While many in Hong Kong would disagree with Li's pro-Beijing sympathies -- including his daughter Gladys, a leading light in Hong Kong's legal establishment, who is openly at odds with her father's political views -- he has had ample opportunity to observe Beijing at close hand.
Li was one of 25 Hong Kong members of a drafting committee charged with framing the Basic Law, the mini-constitution for post-colonial Hong Kong.
He is also a vice-chairman of the Beijing-appointed panel that is working on the power structures of the Special Administrative Region of China that Hong Kong will become next July.

Before Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty became this territory's preoccupation, Li Fook-sean, to give him his full Chinese name, carved out a distinguished career in the territory's legal fraternity.
He studied law in London between 1947 and 1950 and started work in the Hong Kong legal department in 1953.
In a judiciary that was long a British-dominated bastion, Li was in 1971 the first ethnic Chinese judge to be appointed to the High Court and in 1984 the first Chinese justice of appeal.
However he was beaten in the race to become the first Chinese Chief Justice by his junior, Ti Liang Yang -- one of his current rivals for the top post-1997 job.
Li is no stranger to controversy, having crossed legal and political swords with two of Hong Kong's most outspoken and popular advocates of democracy, Martin Lee and Szeto Wah.
He has also suffered personal tragedy, his second son Joseph dying suddenly in Britain in 1995.
According to a popularity poll in late October, only 3.3 percent of Hong Kong people would choose Li to be their leader.
Ahead of him was shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa with 30.2 percent, Yang with 27.5 percent, and bluechip businessman Peter Woo with 8.7 percent.
However, it is not ordinary Hong Kong people who will make the choice. That duty goes to a 400-strong Beijing-supervised group expected to hand down their decision in mid-December.
